items.summary: The First Circuit issued an opinion by Judge Dunlap in United States v. Newton, No. 25-1101, affirming the judgment of the District of Massachusetts. A jury convicted Faith Newton of one count of conspiracy to commit health care fraud, one count of health care fraud, and three counts of money laundering, and the district court imposed a 144-month term of imprisonment. On appeal, Newton challenged the grant of self-representation at trial, the denial of suppression for cell phone data obtained by Customs and Border Protection at Boston Logan Airport, and the loss calculation and sophisticated means enhancement at sentencing, and the court stated that none of these arguments succeeded.

UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE THIRD CIRCUIT
No. 22-1499
MS. LINDA MIGLIORI; FRANCIS J. FOX; RICHARD E. RICHARDS; KENNETH RINGER;
SERGIO RIV AS,
APPELLANTS

ZACHARY COHEN,
INTERVENOR

v.

LEHIGH COUNTY BOARD OF ELECTIONS

DA VID RIT
items.summary: In this nonprecedential opinion, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit affirmed a district court's award of attorneys' fees under 42 U.S.C. § 1988 to Linda Migliori and four other voter plaintiffs in their suit against the Lehigh County Board of Elections. The court held that the plaintiffs were a prevailing party, that the Board's objections met the specificity standard of Bell v. United Princeton Properties, Inc., that the district court's hours reduction and its Allentown market-rate determination were within its discretion and not clear error, and that fees for litigating the fee petition were properly denied because no lodestar analysis was submitted. Judge Matey, dissenting, would hold that the plaintiffs have no cause of action under 52 U.S.C. § 10101(a)(2)(B), would find that special circumstances preclude a fee award, and would vacate the judgment and remand.

items.summary: This nonprecedential opinion, filed October 29, 2026, addresses the Official Committee of Unsecured Creditors' appeal in the Invitae Corporation bankruptcy, which challenged the denial of its motion for derivative standing and the confirmation of Invitae's reorganization plan containing releases. The Third Circuit affirmed the district court's affirmance of the Bankruptcy Court's orders. It held that the Bankruptcy Court did not abuse its discretion in its cost-benefit analysis, which found that the costs of the Committee's proposed claims outweighed their likely benefits to the estate.

items.summary: This nonprecedential opinion, filed October 29, 2026, addresses the Lehigh County Board of Elections' appeal and the plaintiff voters' cross-appeal, both arising from the district court's order granting in part and denying in part attorneys' fees under 42 U.S.C. § 1988. The Third Circuit affirmed, finding the Board's objections sufficiently specific, the hour reduction within the district court's discretion, the Allentown rate determination free of clear error, and the denial of fees for the fee petition supported by the record. Judge Matey dissented, stating that the plaintiffs had no cause of action under 52 U.S.C. § 10101(a)(2)(B) and that fees should be denied or the judgment vacated.

items.summary: The Tenth Circuit affirmed the Northern District of Oklahoma's dismissal of Tamar Jackson's pro se 42 U.S.C. § 1983 suit against Derrick Yazel and Misty Cornwell, officials at the Northeast Oklahoma Community Correctional Center, which alleged denial of access to the courts and retaliation. items.summary: The Tenth Circuit affirmed in part the dismissal of a pro se plaintiff's § 1983 and Title II ADA claims arising from a Kansas state family-law proceeding, which named a state district judge, the state district court, its chief judge, and Johnson County. items.summary: The Tenth Circuit affirmed the district court's denial of the Ute Indian Tribe's motion to intervene in a Clean Air Act enforcement action brought by the United States and Utah against Ovintiv's successor, FourPoint Resources. The district court had ruled that the Tribe lacked Article III standing to seek to set aside the consent decree, which required a $5,500,000 civil penalty and emissions mitigation, based on the United States' alleged failure to consult with the Tribe. The panel held that the Tribe did not show an injury in fact to its sovereign, quasi-sovereign, or economic interests, and it did not reach the United States' alternative grounds for affirmance.

items.summary: In California Chamber of Commerce v. Bonta, the Ninth Circuit affirmed a preliminary injunction blocking enforcement of California Senate Bill 399 (Cal. Lab. Code § 1137(c)), which prohibits employers from taking adverse action against employees who decline to attend employer-sponsored meetings or communications about religious or political matters. The panel held that the Western Growers Association had standing and that the industry groups were likely to succeed on their First Amendment claim, applying strict scrutiny and rejecting the captive audience justification for content-based restrictions on nongovernmental speech. The panel did not reach the preemption claim under the National Labor Relations Act.
items.title: CALIFORNIA CHAMBER OF COMMERCE, ET AL. V. BONTA, ET AL.

items.summary: In Red Eagle Law, L.C. v. Rubio, the Ninth Circuit granted the government's emergency motion for a stay pending appeal of a preliminary injunction that had required the State Department to reopen registration for the fiscal year 2027 Diversity Visa Program. The per curiam order held that the plaintiff law firm is not within the zone of interests of the Diversity Visa Program statute and does not have a cause of action, and it stated that the court does not endorse the Department's failure to open the registration period. Judge N. Randy Smith concurred, writing that the plaintiff also lacks Article III standing.

items.summary: In Maplebear Inc. (Instacart), et al. v. City of Seattle, the Ninth Circuit issued the same superseding amended opinion and dissent in this companion appeal (No. 25-231), consolidated with No. 25-228, affirming the denial of a preliminary injunction against Seattle's App-Based Worker Deactivation Rights Ordinance. The majority held that the ordinance's written-notice requirement meets the Zauderer test, that the 'reasonably related' requirement regulates speech concerning unlawful deactivations, and that the ordinance is not unconstitutionally vague. Judge Bennett dissented in part, stating that the ordinance compels speech and would vacate and remand.

City of Seattle, the Ninth Circuit withdrew its March 4, 2026 opinion and issued a superseding amended opinion and dissent affirming the denial of a preliminary injunction against Seattle's App-Based Worker Deactivation Rights Ordinance. The majority held that the ordinance's requirement that network companies inform workers in writing of their deactivation policies meets the Zauderer test, that the 'reasonably related' requirement regulates speech concerning unlawful deactivations, and that the ordinance is not unconstitutionally vague. Judge Bennett dissented in part, stating that the ordinance compels speech and would vacate and remand for further proceedings.

items.summary: In Colvin & Son, LLC v. Burgum, the Ninth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for federal defendants in a challenge to two Bureau of Land Management gather plans for removing excess wild horses in Nye County, Nevada, covering the Little Fish Lake Joint Management Area and the Stone Cabin Complex. The panel held that the Wild Horses Act requires BLM to remove excess animals as promptly as logistically and reasonably possible, and that the Act does not require a specific time frame for removal actions. The court rejected Laykovich's facial Second Amendment challenge, holding that the provision has at least some constitutional applications. Fortson challenged the denial of a pretrial continuance, the denial of a motion to suppress evidence from a warrantless parole search of an apartment, and the admission of post-arrest interview statements. The court found no abuse of discretion in the continuance ruling because Fortson did not show actual prejudice, and it found no reversible error in the remaining challenges.

items.summary: The Fourth Circuit, in an unpublished per curiam opinion in United States v. Gibbs (No. 24-4150), affirmed a 204-month sentence imposed after a guilty plea to possession of a firearm and ammunition by a convicted felon, where the Armed Career Criminal Act mandatory minimum was 180 months and the advisory Guidelines range was 188-235 months. The court found that the district court did not base the sentence on a detective's testimony about a child's death, because the district court repeatedly stated it was not holding the defendant responsible for that death. The court also rejected a substantive reasonableness challenge raised for the first time on appeal regarding the defendant's youth, concluding that the within-Guidelines sentence was presumptively reasonable and the defendant had not rebutted that presumption.

items.summary: In an unpublished per curiam opinion dated December 24, 2025, the Fifth Circuit considered the government's motion to dismiss the appeal of Rashon Jermaine Harris, who challenged a 240-month sentence and three years of supervised release imposed after a guilty plea to possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine. The court held that the plea agreement's appeal waiver was knowing and voluntary and applied to the appeal, and it found the challenges foreclosed by circuit precedent, including the majority opinion in United States v. Melancon. The government's motion to dismiss was granted, its alternative motion for summary affirmance was denied, and the appeal was dismissed.
items.title: USA v. Harris

items.summary: On remand from the Supreme Court, the Fifth Circuit issued an opinion dated October 29, 2026 in the appeal of Rashon Jermaine Harris, applying Hunter v. United States (2026), which holds that an appeal waiver is unenforceable when enforcing it would result in a miscarriage of justice. The court found that the appeal waiver was knowing and voluntary, that the same-day timing of the guilty plea did not undermine it, and that application of the U.S.S.G. § 3C1.2 enhancement did not constitute a miscarriage of justice, noting that standard-fare sentencing errors cannot cancel an appeal waiver. The court enforced the appeal waiver and dismissed the appeal.
items.title: USA v. Harris

items.summary: In an unpublished per curiam opinion dated October 29, 2026, the Fifth Circuit addressed the appeal of Afrika Roshawn Seals from the denial of a motion to dismiss the indictment and from a 292-month within-guidelines sentence imposed after a guilty plea. The court held that the indictment established probable cause, so a preliminary hearing was not required under Gerstein v. Pugh, and it found no clear error in the district court's application of three two-level enhancements under U.S.S.G. §§ 2D1.1(b)(1), 2D1.1(b)(12), and 3C1.1 based on the record. The court also rejected the substantive reasonableness challenge and affirmed the judgment.
items.title: USA v. Seals

items.summary: In an unpublished per curiam opinion dated October 29, 2026, the Fifth Circuit addressed the appeal of Pedro Garcia Lopez, who was convicted and sentenced under the enhanced penalty provision of 8 U.S.C. § 1326(b)(2). The court acknowledged that Lopez's prior deferred adjudication probation meant no aggravated felony conviction preceded removal, but it found no effect on substantial rights under plain error review, upheld the supervised release term as individually assessed and within the statutory range, and noted that a constitutional challenge to the § 1326(b) recidivism enhancement is foreclosed. The conviction and sentence were affirmed, and the case was remanded for reformation of the written judgment to reflect a conviction under § 1326(b)(1) rather than the cited § 1326(a) and (b)(2).
items.title: USA v. Lopez

items.summary: In an unpublished per curiam opinion dated October 29, 2026, the Fifth Circuit addressed the appeal of Robert Leon Donaldson, a pro se plaintiff whose Title VII complaint was before the Northern District of Texas. The court determined that it lacked jurisdiction because the record contained no evidence of consent to proceed before a magistrate judge and because a magistrate judge's report and recommendation is not a final decision under 28 U.S.C. § 1291. The court denied leave to proceed in forma pauperis and the motion for equitable tolling, and dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction.

Severino (No. 25-13996), granted the government's motion for summary affirmance and affirmed the district court's orders denying a pro se defendant's motion for a sentence reduction under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(2) based on Amendment 821 and denying his motion for reconsideration. items.summary: The Eleventh Circuit, in an unpublished per curiam opinion in United States v. Smith (No. 25-14413), affirmed the conviction for possession of a firearm by a convicted felon and the denial of a motion to suppress evidence from a warrantless vehicle search. The defendant argued for the first time on appeal that, under recent changes to Florida marijuana law, the odor of marijuana alone cannot establish probable cause, and the court reviewed that new theory for plain error. The court held that binding circuit precedent in United States v. Tobin and United States v. Harden treats the smell of marijuana alone as establishing probable cause, so no plain error occurred.

items.summary: The Federal Circuit, in a nonprecedential opinion in Polich v. Collins (No. 2025-1299), dismissed an appeal from the United States Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims concerning a disability rating for traumatic brain injury and PTSD. items.summary: The Federal Circuit, in a nonprecedential opinion in BT Americas, Inc. v. Palo Alto Networks, Inc. (No. 2025-1572), affirmed a Patent Trial and Appeal Board final written decision holding claims 1-25 of U.S. Patent No. 7,895,641 unpatentable as obvious under 35 U.S.C. § 103. The court held that substantial evidence supported the Board's findings that the Duvall and Chu references teach dynamic modification of a probe's analysis capability, that a skilled artisan would have been motivated to combine them, and that the claimed analysis at a secure operations center was identified. The court also held, following Apple Inc. v. Gesture Technology Partners, that the Board had jurisdiction over a patent that expired before the petition was filed.

items.summary: In this per curiam opinion, the Eleventh Circuit denies in part and dismisses in part Toral Baldevbhai Patel's petition for review of a Board of Immigration Appeals order denying her motion to reopen removal proceedings. The court states that the motion was filed more than 90 days after the removal order became final, and that changes in personal circumstances, including deferred action, employment authorization, and a pending U visa application, do not qualify under the changed country conditions exception in 8 U.S.C. 1229a(c)(7)(C)(ii). The court further holds that the Board did not abuse its discretion, that Patel did not show the substantial prejudice required for a due process claim, and that it lacks jurisdiction to review the Board's refusal to reopen sua sponte.
items.title: Toral Patel v. U.S. Attorney General

items.opening_verbatim: Public Law 119–68: To direct the Secretary of the Interior to convey certain Federal land in Arizona to La Paz County, Arizona, and for other purposes. Public Law 68 Public Law 119–68 139 Stat. 1994 2025-12-29 2025-12-29 United States Gover
items.summary: Public Law 119–68, approved December 29, 2025 as H.R. 1043 and cited as the La Paz County Solar Energy and Job Creation Act, directs the Secretary of the Interior to convey approximately 3,400 acres of Bureau of Land Management-managed federal land in La Paz County, Arizona, to the county upon its request. The conveyance is made at fair market value determined by appraisal, excludes lands containing significant cultural, environmental, wildlife, or recreational resources, and withdraws the land from the mining and mineral leasing laws. The county must pay the appraised value and conveyance costs, meet Tribal artifact protection conditions, and deposit sale proceeds in the Federal Land Disposal Account.
items.title: Public Law 119–68: To direct the Secretary of the Interior to convey certain Federal land in Arizona to La Paz County, Arizona, and for other purposes.

items.summary: This regulation establishes exemptions from the requirement of a tolerance for residues of dimethyl sulfoxide (CAS Reg. No. 67-68-5) when used as an inert ingredient (solvent/cosolvent) in pesticide formulations applied to growing crops or to raw agricultural commodities after harvest, in pesticide formulations applied to animals, and in antimicrobial formulations applied to food-contact surfaces in public eating places, dairy-processing equipment, and food-processing equipment and utensils. Spring Regulatory Sciences on behalf of Gaylord Chemical Company, LLC submitted a petition to EPA under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FFDCA), requesting establishment of exemptions from the requirement of a tolerance. This regulation eliminates the need to establish maximum permissible levels for residues of dimethyl sulfoxide when used in accordance with the terms of those exemptions.
items.title: Dimethyl Sulfoxide in Pesticide Formulations; Exemptions From the Requirement of a Tolerance

items.summary: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is classifying the software-aided adjunctive diagnostic device for use by physicians on lesions suspicious for skin cancer into class II (special controls). The special controls that apply to the device type are identified in this order and will be part of the codified language for classification of the software-aided adjunctive diagnostic device for use by physicians on lesions suspicious for skin cancer. We are taking this action because we have determined that classifying the device into class II will provide a reasonable assurance of the safety and effectiveness of the device. We believe this action will also enhance patients' access to beneficial innovative devices, in part by reducing regulatory burdens.

We are taking this action because we have determined that classifying the device into class II will provide a reasonable assurance of the safety and effectiveness of the device. We believe this action will also enhance patients' access to beneficial innovative devices, in part by reducing regulatory burdens.

items.summary: On July 24, 2026, the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved a new drug application for Simtriyo (centanafadine) for the treatment of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in adults and pediatric patients aged 6 years and older, weighing at least 20 kg. The Department of Health and Human Services provided the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) with a scheduling recommendation to place centanafadine, chemically known as (1R,5S)-1-(naphthalen-2-yl)-3-azabicyclo[3.1.0]hexane, in schedule III of the Controlled Substances Act (CSA). In accordance with the CSA, as amended by the Improving Regulatory Transparency for New Medical Therapies Act, DEA is hereby issuing an interim final rule placing centanafadine, including its salts, isomers (whether optical, positional, or geometric), and salts of such isomers whenever the existence of such salts, isomers, and salts of isomers is possible in schedule III of the CSA.

items.summary: Proclamation 11076, dated October 23, 2026, modifies the scope of Canadian products subject to the additional 50 percent ad valorem duties imposed under Proclamation 11048, as amended, pursuant to section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930. Products listed in Annex I, Part A are no longer subject to those duties, and products listed in Annex I, Part B become subject to them, effective with goods entered on or after 12:01 a.m. eastern time on October 30, 2026. The proclamation also modifies the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States as provided in Annex II, directs U.S. Customs and Border Protection to issue implementing rules, and delegates approval authority to the United States Trade Representative under 19 U.S.C. 1338(h).
items.title: Further Modifying the Scope of Products of Canada Subject to the Additional Duties Imposed To Offset Canadian Discrimination Against the Commerce of the United States With Respect to Motor Vehicles

items.summary: H.R. 7254 would amend Section 5(c) of the National Trails System Act (16 U.S.C. 1244(c)) to add the Bay Area Ridge National Scenic Trail, described as a multi-use trail of approximately 550 miles along ridgelines around the San Francisco Bay Area. It directs the Secretary of the Interior to complete and submit to Congress a feasibility study for designating the trail within 3 years of enactment, in consultation with interested organizations including the Bay Area Ridge Trail Council and with each federal and state agency whose lands the trail crosses. The Secretary may complete the study by reviewing and certifying a study prepared by interested organizations, and may consider previous National Park Service and other studies.
items.title: 119 HR 7254 RH: To amend the National Trails System Act to direct the Secretary of the Interior to conduct a study on the feasibility of designating the Bay Area Ridge National Scenic Trail, and for other purposes.

items.summary: H.R. 7954, the Don Young Doug LaMalfa Indian Buffalo Management Act, sets out congressional findings and purposes regarding buffalo management and reestablishment on Indian land. It directs the Secretary of the Interior to consult with Indian Tribes and Tribal organizations, to enter into contracts, cooperative agreements, and grants for buffalo restoration and management activities, and to provide technical assistance. The bill also requires protection of information identified by Tribes as culturally sensitive, proprietary, or confidential, authorizes the transfer of surplus buffalo from federal land to Tribes with possible waiver of charges, states that treaty rights are not altered, and sunsets the authority 7 years after enactment.
items.title: 119 HR 7954 RH: Don Young Doug LaMalfa Indian Buffalo Management Act

items.summary: H.R. 8195, the Responsible Cormorant Management and Control Act of 2026, directs the Secretary of the Interior, acting through the Director of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, to issue regulations within 1 year of enactment for regional management frameworks governing the take of double-crested cormorants. Each framework must address allowable methods and time periods of take, annual public reporting of take, measures to avoid non-target birds, non-lethal measures, and authorized entities, among other requirements. The bill also requires population surveys and framework updates every 5 years, a report on the feasibility of issuing cormorant hunting licenses within 90 days of enactment, and provides that the Act has no force or effect beginning January 1, 2034.
items.title: 119 HR 8195 RH: Responsible Cormorant Management and Control Act of 2026

items.summary: H.R. 8483, the Barona Group of Capitan Grande Band of Mission Indians Land Transfer Act of 2026, transfers administrative jurisdiction of approximately 683 acres of Forest Service land (Parcels 2 and 3) to the Secretary of the Interior and takes that land, together with approximately 164 acres of Bureau of Land Management land (Parcel 1), into trust for the Barona Group of Capitan Grande Band of Mission Indians. The land becomes part of the Tribe's reservation, subject to existing rights, Forest Service administrative vehicular access, continuing public recreational access, and emergency and fuels-management access. The bill prohibits class II and class III gaming on the transferred land, states that existing water rights are not altered, and requires the Tribe to maintain the fuel break in accordance with Forest Service standards.

items.summary: H.R. 9785, the South Dakota Water Feasibility Studies Act, as reported with an amendment, directs the Secretary of the Interior to conduct feasibility studies for three proposed Missouri River basin municipal, rural, and industrial water supply projects: the Western Dakota Regional Water System, the Lewis and Clark Regional Water System expansion, and the Dakota Mainstem Water Supply Project. For the first two studies, the Secretary must submit a feasibility report with a recommendation and a non-Federal cost share of at least 25 percent, and for the third study the Secretary may proceed through a cooperative agreement. items.summary: H.R. 10136, the Crossett Experimental Forest Act of 2026, directs the Secretary of Agriculture to convey the Crossett Experimental Forest, the R.R. Reynolds Research Natural Area, and associated facilities to the State of Arkansas by quitclaim deed without consideration, if the State submits a written request within 180 days of enactment. The State must pay conveyance costs, designate the land as the Crossett Experimental State Forest, and use it for forest research, education, and demonstration in coordination with the University of Arkansas at Monticello and the University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture. If the State fails to meet these conditions and does not correct the failure within 180 days after written notice, the Secretary may revert the land to the United States, and the Forest Service must provide the State with copies of related research records.

items.summary: H.R. 3331, the Mariner Exam Modernization Act, amends Section 7510 of title 46, United States Code, concerning merchant mariner credential examination working groups. The bill adds required members to the working group, including individuals who passed the examination within the prior five years and a representative of the United States Merchant Marine Academy, and requires the Commandant to convene the group annually or when new questions are created. It also requires a review of the examination within 270 days, a plan to update and modernize the examination within 270 days after that review, a prohibition on using new questions until the working group approves them, and a Coast Guard briefing to congressional committees within one year of enactment.

items.summary: S. 675, the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library Act, authorizes the Secretary of the Interior to provide grants of up to $50,000,000 to the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library Foundation for establishing the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library in Medora, North Dakota, subject to appropriations. Grants may not be provided until the Foundation certifies it has received at least $100,000,000 from State of North Dakota funds or non-Federal sources, and grant funds may not be used for the library's maintenance or operation. The Act also authorizes the Secretary, within 180 days of enactment, to enter into agreements to loan Federal museum artifacts and objects from Interior agencies to the Foundation without monetary consideration, and states that no Federal entity is involved in the library's operation unless requested by the non-Federal operator.
items.title: 119 S675 RH: Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library Act
